chapters.title: Chapter 4: Convexity: Where Duration Falls Short

lessons.title: Measuring Convexity and Applying the Convexity Adjustment

children.text: The last lesson showed that duration misses by 9% to 15% on a 30-year G-Sec when yields move 300 basis points. You could reprice the bond from scratch every time, but that defeats the purpose of having a quick risk measure. Instead, bond professionals add a second number next to duration: convexity. With both in hand, a two-term formula estimates price changes almost exactly for moves of 100 or even 200 basis points. This lesson shows you how to calculate convexity by hand, how to get it from any spreadsheet, and how much it sharpens your estimates.

body.text: Duration gives the straight line; convexity adds the bend. Together they turn a rough estimate into a near-exact one: price change ≈ −duration × Δy + ½ × convexity × Δy².

children.text: The Two-Term Price Estimate

body.caption: Δy as a decimal (100 bps = 0.01). The first term is the duration estimate. The second, the convexity adjustment, is always positive for an ordinary bond because Δy² is positive whether yields rise or fall.

markDefs.definition: The extra percentage price change, beyond the duration estimate, that comes from the curvature of the price-yield relationship: ½ × convexity × (change in yield)².

children.text: The second term is the
convexity adjustment
. When yields rise, it makes the loss smaller than duration alone predicts. When yields fall, it makes the gain larger. That is exactly the pattern you saw in the error tables of the last lesson.
Calculating Convexity by Hand

Convexity is calculated from the same cash flows as duration, with one change: instead of weighting each cash flow by its time t, you weight it by t × (t + 1), and discount it by two extra periods. Then divide by the price and by m² to express it in years squared.

body.caption: t = period number, m = coupons per year, y = yield to maturity, P = price. For annual-coupon bonds m = 1; for G-Secs m = 2.

children.text: Take the illustrative 3-year NCD from Chapter 3: 8% annual coupon, priced at par (₹100) at an 8% yield, with a modified duration of 2.58.

body.caption: Convexity of a 3-year 8% annual-coupon NCD at an 8% yield (per ₹100 face value)

children.text: Divide the total by the price and m²: 930.0185 ÷ (100 × 1²) = 9.30. Now test it. If yields jump 200 basis points to 10%, duration alone predicts −2.5771 × 0.02 = −5.154%. The convexity adjustment adds ½ × 9.30 × 0.02² = +0.186%, giving −4.968%. Reprice the NCD at 10% and you get ₹95.03, a fall of 4.974%. The two-term estimate is within 0.01 percentage point.

body.title: Apply the convexity adjustment
body.prompt: An illustrative 10-year G-Sec has a modified duration of 7.10 and a convexity of 64. Yields rise by 150 basis points. Using duration and convexity, estimate the percentage price change. Round to two decimal places, and include the minus sign.
body.explanation: Duration term: −7.10 × 0.015 = −10.65%. Convexity term: ½ × 64 × 0.015² = 0.0072, or +0.72%. Estimate: −10.65% + 0.72% = −9.93%. Duration alone would have overstated the loss by 0.72 percentage points.

children.text: Fixing the 30-Year G-Sec Estimates

Return to the illustrative 30-year 7% G-Sec at par from the last lesson. Its modified duration is 12.47 and, using the same formula with 60 half-year periods, its convexity is 251.2. Here is what the adjustment does to the estimates that went so badly wrong.

body.title: 30-Year G-Sec: Three Views of the Same Price Change (%)

children.text: At ±100 basis points, the error drops from over 1% to about 0.1%. At ±200, from 4% to 6% down to under 1%. Even at ±300 basis points on a 30-year bond, the worst case, the error shrinks by about three-quarters. For a 5-year bond the fix is almost perfect: the 7.10% G-Sec from Chapter 1, with a convexity of 20.97, is estimated at −11.53% for a 300 bp rise against an actual −11.58%.

body.title: Sign of the adjustment
body.question: For an ordinary fixed-coupon bond, what does the convexity adjustment do when yields fall by 100 basis points?
options: It reduces the estimated gain, because yields moved down
It increases the estimated gain, because the adjustment is always positive for an ordinary bond
It has no effect, because convexity only matters when yields rise
It flips the sign of the estimate
body.explanation: The adjustment is ½ × C × Δy². Squaring Δy makes it positive whether yields rise or fall, and C is positive for an ordinary bond. So it always adds to the estimate: a bigger gain when yields fall, a smaller loss when yields rise.

children.text: What Makes Convexity Bigger
The same three drivers that lengthen duration also increase convexity, but maturity has a much stronger effect, because convexity weights cash flows by roughly time squared.

body.caption: Convexity of illustrative bonds at a 7% yield (semi-annual convention)

children.text: Longer maturity:
tripling a zero-coupon bond's maturity from 10 to 30 years multiplies its convexity nearly nine times, from 98.0 to 854.2.
Lower coupon:
among 10-year bonds at 7%, convexity is 98.0 for a zero, 69.9 for a 5% coupon, 64.3 for 7% and 60.1 for 9%.
Lower yield:
the 30-year 7% G-Sec has a convexity of 316.1 at a 5% yield, 251.2 at 7% and 196.9 at 9%.

body.title: Why the adjustment is always positive
body.textWithBlank: The convexity adjustment is positive whether yields rise or fall because it multiplies convexity by the change in yield ___.
body.explanation: Any change in yield, positive or negative, becomes positive when squared. So for an ordinary bond with positive convexity, the adjustment always adds to the duration estimate.

children.text: Getting Convexity from a Spreadsheet

markDefs.definition: Convexity estimated by repricing a bond at a slightly lower and slightly higher yield and measuring how the price curve bends, rather than from a cash flow formula. It also works for bonds whose cash flows change with yields.

children.text: Excel and Google Sheets have DURATION and MDURATION, but no CONVEXITY function. The practical workaround is
effective convexity

: price the bond three times with the PRICE function, at today's yield and at small moves either side, and plug the three prices into one formula. It is the partner of the effective duration you met in Chapter 3.

body.title: Calculate effective convexity
body.prompt: An illustrative 10-year 7% G-Sec trades at ₹100.00 at a 7% yield. Repriced at 6.90%, it is worth ₹100.71385; at 7.10%, ₹99.29258. Using Δy = 0.001, what is its effective convexity? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Numerator: 100.71385 + 99.29258 − 2 × 100 = 0.00643. Denominator: 100 × 0.001² = 0.0001. Effective convexity = 0.00643 ÷ 0.0001 = 64.3. Tiny price differences drive this number, so always keep at least five decimal places in the prices.

body.text: Check the scale before using anyone else's convexity number. This course quotes convexity in years squared, so the 30-year G-Sec's convexity is 251.2 and you plug Δy in as a decimal. Some analytics platforms and reports divide by 100 and would show the same bond as 2.51, to be used with Δy in percentage points. Some also leave out the ½ in the formula. Mixing conventions can make the adjustment 100 times too big or too small, so confirm which one a number follows before applying it.

body.title: Farah's ₹3 crore stress test
body.scenario: Farah Qureshi, a 50-year-old business owner in Lucknow, holds ₹3 crore market value of an illustrative 20-year 7.20% G-Sec, trading at ₹99.48 at a 7.25% yield. Her adviser's risk report shows a modified duration of 10.49 and a convexity of 161.2. She wants to know what happens to her holding if yields move 150 basis points in either direction.
body.prompt: Estimate the percentage and rupee change for a 150 bp rise and a 150 bp fall, first with duration alone and then with duration plus convexity. Given actual repriced changes of −14.07% and +17.72%, which estimate should the adviser use, and why does it matter for Farah?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Duration only: ±10.49 × 0.015 = ±15.73%, or about ±₹47.2 lakh on ₹3 crore.
2. Convexity adjustment: ½ × 161.2 × 0.015² = +1.81%.
3. Duration plus convexity: rise = −15.73% + 1.81% = −13.92%, about −₹41.8 lakh; fall = +15.73% + 1.81% ≈ +17.55% (17.54% from the rounded figures, 17.55% unrounded), about +₹52.6 lakh.
4. Actual: rise = −14.07% (−₹42.2 lakh); fall = +17.72% (+₹53.2 lakh).
5. The two-term estimate is within about 0.15 to 0.17 percentage points of the truth, roughly ₹45,000 to ₹52,000. Duration alone is off by about 1.7 to 2.0 percentage points, roughly ₹5 to ₹6 lakh in each direction.
6. Why it matters: duration alone tells Farah her downside and upside are symmetric at about ₹47 lakh. The convexity-adjusted view shows the reality: about ₹42 lakh of downside against about ₹53 lakh of upside. That asymmetry is valuable information when she decides how much of her wealth to hold in long bonds, and the adviser should report duration and convexity together for any move of 100 bps or more.

cards.definition: ½ × convexity × Δy². Always positive for an ordinary bond.
(P₋ + P₊ − 2P₀) ÷ (P₀ × Δy²). Calculated from three prices.
Higher for longer maturities (roughly with time squared), lower coupons and lower yields.
Some sources quote convexity divided by 100 or omit the ½. Check the convention first.

points: Price change ≈ −modified duration × Δy + ½ × convexity × Δy². The second term corrects duration's straight line.
Convexity uses the same cash flows as duration, weighted by t × (t + 1) and discounted two extra periods.
The 3-year 8% NCD has a convexity of 9.30, and the two-term estimate matched its actual −4.97% fall for a 200 bp rise.
For the 30-year G-Sec (convexity 251.2), the error at ±100 bps drops from over 1% to about 0.1%.
Convexity rises sharply with maturity, and is higher for lower coupons and lower yields.
Spreadsheets have no convexity function; use effective convexity from three PRICE calculations, and always check a number's scale.

Duration and convexity estimates assume an immediate, parallel shift in yields and no change in credit spreads or liquidity. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
